articles.title: How to Clear IGN Notes at Stanley Mosk Courthouse
articles.text: If you're handling a probate case in Los Angeles County, you'll inevitably encounter probate notes, the court's list of items to clear before your hearing. This guide explains exactly what they are and how to clear them.What Are IGN Notes?Probate notes are posted on the court's website before your hearing by the probate examiners at the Stanley Mosk Courthouse. Their Matters To Clear section lists the documents the court still needs.The Los Angeles Superior Court files and hears probate cases at Stanley Mosk (except in the North District, which may use the Antelope Valley Courthouse in Lancaster). Probate examiners review filings before the judge sees them, and post notes when anything is missing.Critical WarningIf the notes are not cleared by the third court day before your hearing, the court may continue the hearing, take it off calendar or deny the petition without prejudice (it can be filed again). This is one of the most common causes of probate delays in LA County.Common Reasons for IGN NotesBased on our experience with hundreds of cases, these are the most common issues that trigger examiner notes:1Missing heir information - Names, addresses, or relationships not properly stated2Bond calculation errors - Incorrect total or missing bond waiver documentation3Inconsistent dates or names - Typos or variations between documents4Missing proof of mailing - DE-121 not properly completed or filed5Publication issues - Newspaper not adjudicated or dates incorrect6Will attachment problems - Original not submitted or copy not certifiedThe 5-Step Process to Clear IGN Notes1Access the Court PortalCheck the LA Superior Court website for probate notes in the days before your scheduled hearing. Navigate to your case and check for any posted examiner notes.2Review Each Note CarefullyRead every note in detail. Each one specifies exactly what information is missing or what correction is needed. Don't skip any, all must be addressed.3Draft Your Verified SupplementPrepare a formal "Supplement to the Petition" that specifically addresses each deficiency. This must be a verified document (signed under penalty of perjury).4Attorney ReviewHave the supplement reviewed by a licensed California probate attorney to ensure it properly addresses all issues and is formatted correctly for the court.5File Before Your HearingFile the supplement by the third court day before your hearing, as the Los Angeles local rules require.What is a Verified Supplement?A Verified Supplement is a formal court document that corrects or adds information to your original Petition for Probate. It must:Reference your case number and the original petitionSpecifically address each examiner noteBe signed under penalty of perjuryInclude any supporting documentation referencedWhy DIY Supplements Often FailMany self-represented executors try to draft their own supplements, but they often fail because:They don't understand the legal terminology used in the notesThey address symptoms rather than root causesThey use incorrect formatting or miss verification requirementsThey file too late for the examiner to review before the hearingHow MyProbateCA Handles IGN NotesOur flat fees ($3,995 full probate, $2,495 simplified) include checking the court's probate notes and preparing the answers before your hearing. When notes appear on your case, we:Monitor the court portal before every hearingDraft professional Verified Supplements addressing each noteHave Attorney Rozsa Gyene (Bar #208356) review itGive it to you to sign and file by the third court day before the hearingKey Takeaways1Check for notes 5-10 days before every hearing2Never appear at a hearing with uncleared notes3File your supplement by the third court day before the hearing4Professional attorney review significantly increases success ratesHave IGN notes on your case? Start your case with MyProbateCA and get professional help clearing them, included in our flat fee ($3,995 for full probate or $2,495 for the simplified home petition).Rozsa Gyene, Esq.California State Bar #208356 • 26+ Years ExperienceRozsa Gyene focuses on California probate administration, with extensive experience at the Stanley Mosk Courthouse in Los Angeles.Verify License Need Help With Your Probate Case?Get attorney-prepared court papers for a flat fee: $3,995 for full probate or $2,495 for the simplified home petition.Explore Our Probate Services→ How Our Process Works→ Probate FAQ (50+ Questions)→ 35 California Locations→ Los Angeles Probate→ San Francisco Probate→ San Diego ProbateRelated ArticlesFees & CostsCalifornia Probate Fees: Statutory vs Flat FeeForms & DocumentsLetters Testamentary California GuideProcessWhat is a Probate Referee?Back to Learning Center

articles.title: California Probate Fees Exposed: Statutory vs Flat Fee
articles.text: One of the biggest shocks for California executors is discovering how much traditional probate attorneys charge. This guide breaks down the statutory fee structure and compares it with our flat fee. On a $500,000 estate, the statutory attorney fee is $13,000. Our flat fee is $3,995 (full probate: $3,995 up to $1,000,000, $5,995 from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000, $7,995 over $2,000,000).What Are Statutory Fees?California Probate Code Section 10810 sets the "statutory" fee schedule that attorneys can charge for probate work. This fee is calculated as a percentage of the gross estate value:Estate ValueFee PercentageFirst $100,0004%Next $100,0003%Next $800,0002%Next $9,000,0001%Next $15,000,0000.5%Above $25,000,000Set by the courtThe Gross Value ProblemHere's what catches most people off guard: statutory fees are calculated on gross value, not net equity. Mortgages, loans, and debts are ignored.Example: The $1M HomeConsider a home worth $1,000,000 with a $900,000 mortgage:Actual equity: $100,000Fee calculation basis: $1,000,000 (gross value)Statutory attorney fee: $23,000, which is 23% of the $100,000 of equity. The personal representative (executor) may also ask for a statutory commission figured the same way. That commission belongs to the personal representative, not to the attorney, and is the same whichever way the court papers are prepared.Fee Comparison by Estate ValueEstate ValueStatutory FeeMyProbateCAYou Save$500,000$13,000$3,995$9,005$750,000$18,000$3,995$14,005$1,000,000$23,000$3,995$19,005$1,500,000$28,000$3,995$24,005$2,000,000$33,000$3,995$29,005These examples are full probate. Our simplified home petition is $2,495. For smaller estates, the total for all ordinary services (the flat fee, the accounting add-on and any uncontested court appearance) never exceeds the statutory fee for the estate's value. You see your exact fee before you pay, and if the inventory value comes in lower, the difference is refunded.Why Are Statutory Fees So High?The statutory fee schedule dates from an era when attorneys hand-typed every document and made multiple trips to the courthouse. Today's technology enables dramatic efficiency, but the fee schedule hasn't changed.Traditional probate attorneys can legally charge these statutory fees, and many do. They're not required to, but it's the easiest path since the fee is pre-approved by the court.Additional Costs Beyond Attorney FeesWhether you use a statutory-fee attorney or MyProbateCA, you'll have these additional third-party costs:Cost TypeTypical AmountWhen DueCourt Filing Fee$435 ($450 in Riverside and San Francisco)At initial filingNewspaper Publication$200-350After filingProbate Referee Fee0.1% of assetsAfter inventoryCertified Copies$25-50 eachAs neededBond Premium (if required)Often about 0.5-1% of the bond per year (estimate)Before hearingHow MyProbateCA Offers $3,995 (or $2,495)Our flat fee of $3,995 for full probate ($2,495 for the simplified home petition) provides attorney-prepared court papers from Rozsa Gyene (Bar #208356) at a fraction of the traditional cost. articles.title: What is a Probate Referee in California?
articles.text: Most California probate cases involve a Probate Referee, a court-appointed official who appraises estate assets (the court can waive the referee for good cause). This guide explains who they are, what they do, and how to work with them effectively.What is a Probate Referee?A Probate Referee is a specially qualified appraiser appointed by the California State Controller to value estate assets for probate proceedings. They're not employees of the court: they're independent professionals licensed to provide official valuations.When you file a Petition for Probate, the court automatically assigns a Probate Referee to your case. You don't choose them: they're assigned on a rotating basis in each county.Key Facts About Probate RefereesAppointmentCourt-AssignedYou don't chooseFee0.1% of assets$75 minimumDeadline4 monthsFrom LettersWhat Does a Probate Referee Appraise?The Probate Referee values all non-cash assets in the estate. This includes:Real estate - Homes, land, commercial property, rental propertiesVehicles - Cars, boats, RVs, motorcyclesSecurities - Stocks, bonds, mutual funds (valued at date of death)Business interests - Ownership in LLCs, partnerships, corporationsPersonal property - Jewelry, art, collectibles, furnitureWhat the Executor ValuesThe executor (not the referee) values cash and cash equivalents: bank accounts, money market accounts, and similar liquid assets. You report these values on the Inventory & Appraisal form.Probate Referee FeesThe Probate Referee charges 0.1% (one-tenth of one percent) of the total assets they appraise, with a minimum fee of $75. This fee is paid from estate funds.Assets AppraisedReferee Fee (0.1%)$100,000$100$500,000$500$1,000,000$1,000$2,000,000$2,000The Inventory & Appraisal ProcessHere's how the process works:1Receive Letters TestamentaryThe 4-month clock for the Inventory & Appraisal starts when you receive your Letters.2Compile Asset ListIdentify all assets that need appraisal and gather supporting documentation (deeds, statements, titles).3Contact the Probate RefereeReach out to the assigned referee with your asset list. They may schedule property inspections if needed.4Receive AppraisalThe referee provides their official valuations, which you incorporate into Form DE-160.5File the Inventory & AppraisalSubmit Form DE-160 to the court within the 4-month deadline, signed by you and the referee.Tips for Working with Probate RefereesStart early - Don't wait until month 3 to contact the refereeBe organized - Provide complete documentation for each assetRespond promptly - Answer the referee's questions quicklyAllow access - If they need to inspect property, schedule it promptlyHow MyProbateCA HelpsOur flat fee ($3,995 for full probate or $2,495 for the simplified home petition) includes the papers and instructions for the Probate Referee step:We identify which assets need referee appraisalWe prepare and organize all documentationWe tell you what the referee needs from you and whenWe prepare Form DE-160 correctly for you to fileNeed help with the Inventory & Appraisal process? articles.title: Letters Testamentary California: Your Golden Ticket Explained
articles.text: Letters Testamentary are the single most important document you'll receive as an executor. Without them, you can't access bank accounts, sell property, or manage estate assets. This guide explains everything you need to know.What Are Letters Testamentary?Letters Testamentary (Form DE-150) are an official court document that proves you have legal authority to act on behalf of the estate. They're issued by the probate court after the judge signs the Order for Probate appointing you as executor.Think of them as your "golden ticket": the document that allows you to:Access and close the decedent's bank accountsSell real estate owned by the estateTransfer vehicle titlesManage investment and brokerage accountsFile tax returns for the estatePay creditors and estate expensesLetters Testamentary vs Letters of AdministrationYou'll hear two terms used:Letters TestamentaryIssued when there is a Will and the person is named as "Executor" in the Will.Letters of AdministrationIssued when there is no Will (intestate) and the person is appointed as "Administrator."Both documents grant the same legal authority: the only difference is the title (Executor vs Administrator) based on whether there's a Will.How to Get Letters TestamentaryHere's the process to obtain Letters:1File Petition for ProbateSubmit Form DE-111 to the Superior Court requesting appointment as executor.2Complete Required NoticesMail the notice of petition to heirs (DE-121) and publish it in a newspaper.3Attend Probate HearingAppear at the scheduled hearing (or add our optional court appearance). The judge signs the Order for Probate.4Request Certified CopiesOrder multiple certified copies of the Letters from the court clerk. You'll need them.How Many Certified Copies Do You Need?Order several certified copies. The court charges $40 to certify each copy plus $0.50 per page, and many institutions keep the copy you give them. Here's why you may need several:•Each bank may require its own copy•Title companies require a copy for each real estate transaction•The DMV needs a copy to transfer vehicle titles•Investment companies typically keep the copy you provide•Keep 1-2 copies for your recordsImportant: Certification Date MattersSome institutions require Letters certified within 60 days. If your Letters are older, you may need to get fresh certified copies from the court.Using Letters with Banks & Financial InstitutionsWhen you visit a bank with Letters Testamentary, you typically need:Certified copy of Letters TestamentaryCertified copy of the Death CertificateYour personal identification (driver's license)Bank's estate account application (they'll provide this)Most banks will open an "Estate Account" where you can consolidate the decedent's funds. This keeps estate money separate from your personal funds, which is legally required.Using Letters to Sell Real EstateTo sell property owned by the estate, the title company will require:Certified Letters Testamentary (recent certification)Proof that you have Independent Administration powers (if applicable)Court confirmation of sale (if you don't have Independent Administration)MyProbateCA Makes It EasyOur flat fee ($3,995 for full probate or $2,495 for the simplified home petition) includes:Preparation of all documents needed to obtain LettersGuidance on how many certified copies to orderInstructions for using Letters with banks and institutionsOptional add-onsOptional attorney appearance at a hearing ($500 per hearing, limited scope representation)Ready to get your Letters Testamentary? Start your case with MyProbateCA and we'll guide you through every step.Rozsa Gyene, Esq.California State Bar #208356 • 26+ Years ExperienceRozsa Gyene focuses on California probate administration, with extensive experience at the Stanley Mosk Courthouse in Los Angeles.Verify License Need Help With Your Probate Case?Get attorney-prepared court papers for a flat fee: $3,995 for full probate or $2,495 for the simplified home petition.Explore Our Probate Services→ How Our Process Works→ Probate FAQ (50+ Questions)→ 35 California Locations→ Los Angeles Probate→ San Francisco Probate→ San Diego ProbateRelated ArticlesProcessWhat is a Probate Referee?Court ProceduresHow to Clear IGN NotesExecutor GuideProbate Bond RequirementsBack to Learning Center

articles.title: Probate Bond Requirements in California: When You Need One
articles.text: One of the most confusing aspects of California probate is the probate bond requirement. This guide explains when bonds are required, how much they cost, and how to potentially avoid them altogether.What is a Probate Bond?A probate bond (also called an "executor bond" or "fiduciary bond") is a type of insurance policy that protects the estate's beneficiaries. If the executor mismanages estate funds or commits fraud, the bond company pays the beneficiaries up to the bond amount.Think of it as protection for the heirs: if something goes wrong, they have financial recourse through the bond company.When is a Bond Required?Under California Probate Code Section 8480, a bond is generally required unless one of the following exceptions applies:Bond Required• Will doesn't waive bond• No will, unless all heirs waive bond in writing• Not all beneficiaries waive bond• Court has concerns about executorBond May Be Waived• Will specifically waives bond• All beneficiaries waive bond in writing• Even then, the court can require a bond for good causeHow Much Does a Probate Bond Cost?The bond amount is typically set at the value of the estate's personal property plus one year's estimated income. The executor doesn't pay the full bond amount: they pay an annual premium to a surety company.Bond AmountAnnual Premium (0.5-1%)$100,000$500 - $1,000/year$250,000$1,250 - $2,500/year$500,000$2,500 - $5,000/year$1,000,000$5,000 - $10,000/yearImportant: Premium Paid from EstateThe bond premium is paid from estate funds, not the executor's personal money. However, it reduces the amount available for distribution to beneficiaries.How to Get a Bond WaiverThere are several ways to avoid the bond requirement:1Will WaiverThe best scenario: If the Will contains language like "I direct that no bond be required of my executor," the court will typically honor this.2Beneficiary ConsentAll beneficiaries can sign a written waiver agreeing that no bond is required. This is filed with the court.3Blocked AccountPlace estate funds in a "blocked account" that requires court permission to access. This protects funds without requiring a bond.4Limited AuthorityRequest limited independent administration powers (no authority to sell real estate without court supervision). This keeps the real estate out of the bond amount, which can lower it.How the Bond Amount is CalculatedThe court calculates the required bond amount using this formula:Personal Property Value + Estimated Annual Income = Bond AmountReal property is not included in the bond calculation unless the executor has full independent administration powers over it.Getting Approved for a Probate BondSurety companies will evaluate the proposed executor before issuing a bond. They typically consider:Credit history - Good credit makes approval easierCriminal background - No felonies or financial crimesFinancial stability - Ability to manage estate responsiblyRelationship to decedent - Family members generally preferredWhat if You Can't Get a Bond?If you're unable to obtain a bond (due to poor credit or other issues), you have options:•Request a blocked account instead of a bond•Have a co-executor who can qualify for the bond•Step aside and let another qualified person serve as executor•Petition the court for waiver with supporting documentationWhen is the Bond Released?The bond remains in effect until the estate is fully administered and the executor is discharged by the court. This happens when:All debts and taxes have been paidAll assets have been distributed to beneficiariesFinal accounting has been approved by the courtOrder for Final Distribution has been signedHow MyProbateCA Helps with BondsOur flat fee ($3,995 full probate) includes assistance with bond requirements:We determine if a bond is required for your caseWe help prepare bond waiver requests when applicableWe can recommend reliable surety companiesWe prepare the papers for a blocked account if the court allows oneKey Takeaways1Probate bonds protect beneficiaries, not the executor2Premium costs 0.5-1% of the bond amount annually3Bonds can often be waived if the Will allows or beneficiaries consent4Blocked accounts are an alternative to posting bondHave questions about bond requirements for your case? Start with MyProbateCA and we'll help determine if a bond is needed and how to minimize costs.Rozsa Gyene, Esq.California State Bar #208356 • 26+ Years ExperienceRozsa Gyene focuses on California probate administration, with extensive experience at the Stanley Mosk Courthouse in Los Angeles.Verify License Need Help With Your Probate Case?Get attorney-prepared court papers for a flat fee: $3,995 for full probate or $2,495 for the simplified home petition.Explore Our Probate Services→ How Our Process Works→ Probate FAQ (50+ Questions)→ 35 California Locations→ Los Angeles Probate→ San Francisco Probate→ San Diego ProbateRelated ArticlesForms & DocumentsLetters Testamentary California GuideFees & CostsCalifornia Probate Fees ExplainedProcessWhat is a Probate Referee?Back to Learning Center

articles.title: How to File Probate in California: Step-by-Step Guide
articles.text: Filing probate in California can seem overwhelming, but it follows a predictable 11-phase process. This guide walks you through exactly what you need to do, from gathering documents to receiving your Letters Testamentary.Before You StartCalifornia probate is usually needed when someone dies owning property in their name alone worth more than $208,850 in total (deaths on or after April 1, 2025), not counting assets that pass outside probate. A primary residence worth up to $750,000 can pass by a simpler court petition, and property going to a surviving spouse may not need probate. If the estate qualifies, you may be able to use a Small Estate Affidavit instead.Step 1: Gather Essential DocumentsBefore filing anything with the court, collect these critical documents:Original Will (if one exists): the court requires the original, not a copyCertified Death Certificates: most families need only a few copies and can order more laterList of Assets: real estate, bank accounts, investments, vehiclesList of Heirs: names, addresses, and relationships of all beneficiaries and legal heirsList of Debts: mortgages, credit cards, medical bills, taxes owedStep 2: Determine Where to FileCalifornia probate must be filed in the Superior Court of the county where the decedent lived at the time of death (their "domicile"). This is true even if they owned property in other counties.Common California Probate CourtsLos Angeles County: Stanley Mosk Courthouse, 111 N. Hill StreetOrange County: Lamoreaux Justice Center, 341 The City DriveSan Diego County: Central Courthouse, 1100 Union StreetSan Francisco: Civic Center Courthouse, 400 McAllister StreetSanta Clara County: Downtown Superior Court, 191 N. First StreetSee all 35 California probate court locations →Step 3: Complete the Petition for Probate (Form DE-111)The Petition for Probate is your formal request to open the estate. This form requires:• Decedent's full legal name and any aliases• Date and place of death• Whether a will exists (and attach it)• Names and addresses of all heirs and beneficiaries• Estimated value of the estate• Name of proposed executor/administrator• Request for authority (full or limited)Common MistakeMany self-filed petitions are rejected because the heir information is incomplete or inconsistent. Every heir must be listed with their exact legal relationship to the decedent.Step 4: File with the Court and Pay FeesSubmit your completed petition to the probate clerk. You'll need to pay the filing fee at this time.California Probate Filing CostsPetition Filing Fee$435 ($450 in Riverside and San Francisco)Newspaper Publication$200 - $350Certified Copies (each)$25 - $50Probate Referee Fee0.1% of assets the referee appraisesSee complete fee breakdown →Step 5: Publish Notice and Mail to HeirsCalifornia law requires two types of notice before the hearing:Newspaper PublicationPublish "Notice of Petition to Administer Estate" three times in a newspaper of general circulation in the city where the decedent lived, the first at least 15 days before the hearing.Mail Notice (DE-121)Mail notice to all heirs and beneficiaries and any executors named in the will at least 15 days before the hearing date. Known creditors get a separate notice after Letters issue.Step 6: Attend the Probate HearingYour first court hearing is often several weeks after filing (an estimate). If filing in Los Angeles County, check the probate notes before your hearing and file any required supplements by the third court day before it.At the hearing, the judge will:• Review your petition for completeness• Confirm proper notice was given• Hear any objections from heirs or creditors• Appoint you as executor/administrator (if approved)• Issue Letters Testamentary or Letters of AdministrationStep 7: After Your Hearing - What's NextOnce appointed, you'll need to complete these remaining phases:7Inventory & AppraisalWork with the court-appointed probate referee to value all estate assets, and file the inventory within 4 months after Letters, along with the certification that the change in ownership statement (BOE-502-D) was filed for any California real estate.8Creditor ManagementNotice known creditors and wait for the claim period to end (4 months after Letters, or 60 days after a mailed notice if later) before paying valid debts.9Tax ReturnsFile the decedent's final personal tax return and estate income tax returns if needed.10Final AccountingPrepare a detailed accounting of all money received and paid by the estate.11Final DistributionObtain court approval and distribute remaining assets to beneficiaries.Need Help Filing?MyProbateCA prepares your California probate court documents for a flat fee of $3,995 ($2,495 for the simplified home petition), saving you $19,000+ compared to statutory attorney fees. We prepare the documents, clear probate notes, and guide you through every step.Start Your Case - FreeHow Long Does California Probate Take?Most California probate cases take 9 to 18 months from filing to final distribution. See our detailed timeline guide for what to expect each month.Timeline FactorsEstimates: simple estates often 9 to 12 months; complex estates or disputes often 18 months or moreRozsa Gyene, Esq.California State Bar #208356 • 26+ Years ExperienceRozsa Gyene focuses on California probate administration, with extensive experience at the Stanley Mosk Courthouse in Los Angeles.Verify License Need Help With Your Probate Case?Get attorney-prepared court papers for a flat fee: $3,995 for full probate or $2,495 for the simplified home petition.Explore Our Probate Services→ How Our Process Works→ Probate FAQ (50+ Questions)→ 35 California Locations→ Los Angeles Probate→ San Francisco Probate→ San Diego ProbateRelated ArticlesFees & CostsCalifornia Probate Fees: Statutory vs Flat FeeForms & DocumentsLetters Testamentary California GuideProcessProbate Timeline California: What to ExpectBack to Learning Center

articles.title: Small Estate Affidavit California: When You Don't Need Probate
articles.text: Not every estate needs to go through California's lengthy probate process. If the estate is small enough, you may be able to transfer assets using a Small Estate Affidavit: a simple form that avoids court entirely.Good NewsCalifornia has some of the most generous small estate thresholds in the country. For deaths on or after April 1, 2025, property worth up to $208,850 in total can be collected without probate, not counting assets that pass outside probate. A primary residence worth up to $750,000 can pass by a simpler court petition.What is a Small Estate Affidavit?A Small Estate Affidavit (also called a "Declaration for Collection of Personal Property") is a legal document that allows you to claim a deceased person's assets without going through probate court. Under California Probate Code Section 13100, qualifying successors can use this affidavit to:Collect bank account fundsTransfer vehicle titlesClaim stocks, bonds, and investment accountsCollect insurance proceeds payable to the estateRetrieve personal property from storage units or safe deposit boxesCalifornia Small Estate Limits (deaths on or after April 1, 2025)Current ThresholdsSmall Estate Affidavit(No court filing required; counts real and personal property)$208,850Primary Residence Petition(Simpler court process; the home only, no limit on other property)$750,000Real Property of Small Value Affidavit(Filed with the court at least 6 months after death)$69,625Spousal Property Petition(For surviving spouses)No LimitNote: The limits depend on the date of death. For deaths from April 1, 2022 through March 31, 2025, the affidavit and residence petition limit was $184,500 and the small value real property limit was $61,500. For deaths before April 1, 2022, they were $166,250 and $55,425. The next adjustment is April 1, 2028.Do You Qualify? Requirements ChecklistTo use a Small Estate Affidavit in California, ALL of the following must be true:40 Days Have PassedAt least 40 days must have elapsed since the decedent's deathNo Probate FiledNo probate proceeding is currently pending or has been conductedUnder the LimitTotal value of the decedent's California real and personal property is $208,850 or less (deaths on or after April 1, 2025), not counting the excluded assets listed belowYou're the Rightful SuccessorYou are entitled to the property under the will or California intestacy lawsReal Estate Counts Toward the LimitReal estate does not rule out the affidavit, but its value counts toward the limit and it needs its own transfer step (see below)What Does Not Count Toward the LimitGood news: many assets are excluded when calculating whether you're under the limit:Excluded from Calculation• Joint tenancy property• Property in a living trust• Life insurance (with named beneficiary)• Retirement accounts (401k, IRA with beneficiary)• Payable-on-death bank accounts• Transfer-on-death securities• All registered vehicles, boats and mobilehomes, whatever their valueIncluded in Calculation• Bank accounts in decedent's name only• Stocks/bonds without TOD designation• Personal property (furniture, jewelry)• Real estate in the decedent's name alone (except a home that passes by a primary residence petition)• Business interests• Money owed to decedentHow to Use a Small Estate Affidavit: Step by StepStep 1: Wait 40 DaysYou cannot use the affidavit until 40 days after the date of death.Step 2: Prepare the AffidavitComplete the "Declaration for Collection of Personal Property" form. Include your information, the decedent's information, description of property, and your legal basis to claim it.Step 3: Attach Required DocumentsInclude a certified copy of the death certificate. If there's a will, attach a copy.Step 4: Sign Under Penalty of PerjuryThe affidavit must be signed and dated. Some institutions require notarization.Step 5: Present to the InstitutionDeliver the affidavit to the bank, brokerage, or other entity holding the property. They must release it within a reasonable time.Important WarningBy signing the affidavit, you become personally liable to creditors, other heirs, and the state of California if you misrepresent the facts or misuse the funds. This is a sworn statement under penalty of perjury.What About Real Estate?Real property (homes, land, commercial buildings) is not transferred with the Small Estate Affidavit for personal property. California offers two simpler options for real estate:Primary Residence PetitionIf the decedent's primary residence in California is worth $750,000 or less (deaths on or after April 1, 2025), the heirs or beneficiaries can ask the court to transfer the home with a simpler petition. It can be filed 40 days after death, and there is no limit on the decedent's other property.Affidavit for Real Property of Small ValueIf all of the decedent's California real estate is worth $69,625 or less (deaths on or after April 1, 2025), an heir or beneficiary can file a notarized affidavit with the court.Requirements: 6 months must pass after death, no probate pending, and funeral costs, last illness costs and unsecured debts must be paid.Small Estate Affidavit vs Full ProbateFactorSmall Estate AffidavitFull ProbateTime Required40 days + processingOften 9 to 18 months (estimate)Court FilingNot requiredRequiredAttorney RequiredNoHighly recommendedCost$0 - $100Our flat fee: $3,995 or less; statutory fees: $23,000+ on a $1M estateAsset Limit$208,850 (deaths on or after April 1, 2025)No limitWhen You Can't Avoid ProbateUnfortunately, a Small Estate Affidavit won't work if:Estate value exceeds $208,850 (deaths on or after April 1, 2025), not counting excluded assetsReal estate is worth more than the limits for the home petition or the small value real property affidavitThere are disputes among heirsCreditors need formal court processThe institution refuses to honor the affidavitEstate Over the Limit?If the estate is over these limits, you will likely need to file probate. articles.title: Probate Timeline California: What to Expect Each Month
articles.text: Quick Summary: California Probate Timeline•Simple estates: often about 9 to 12 months (estimate)•Average estates: often about 12 to 18 months (estimate)•Complex estates: often 18 months or more (estimate)•Required by law: the creditor claim period (4 months after Letters, or 60 days after a mailed notice if later) and a petition to close or a status report within 1 year after LettersOverview: How Long Does Probate Take in California?California probate typically takes between 9 and 18 months for most estates. However, this timeline can vary significantly based on the complexity of the estate, whether there are disputes, and the efficiency of the local probate court.One thing that cannot change is the creditor claim period: 4 months after Letters are issued, or 60 days after a mailed notice of administration if that is later (California Probate Code Section 9100). Even the simplest estate cannot close before it ends.Understanding the probate timeline helps executors and beneficiaries set realistic expectations and plan accordingly. While you can't eliminate the waiting periods, working with an experienced probate attorney familiar with your local court can help minimize unnecessary delays.Important: If the estate qualifies for a small estate affidavit ($208,850 or less for deaths on or after April 1, 2025), you may be able to avoid probate entirely and transfer assets in as little as 40 days after death.Month-by-Month California Probate TimelineBelow is a detailed breakdown of what typically happens during each phase of California probate. Keep in mind that these timeframes can overlap and may vary based on your specific situation.Initial Filing & PetitionMonth 1Locate the original will and deliver it to the court clerk within 30 days after learning of the deathIdentify heirs and beneficiariesInventory assets for the petitionFile Petition for Probate with the Superior CourtPay the filing fee ($435 in Los Angeles and most counties; $450 in Riverside and San Francisco)Schedule hearing date (typically 30-45 days out)Pro Tip: Whoever has the original will must deliver it to the superior court clerk within 30 days after learning of the death (unless a petition is filed first). There is no 30-day deadline to file the petition itself.Notice & PublicationMonth 2Mail Notice of Petition to all heirs and beneficiariesPublish the Notice of Petition to Administer Estate three times in a local newspaper, the first at least 15 days before the hearingFile Proof of Service with the courtPrepare for probate hearingPro Tip: Use a newspaper of general circulation in the city where the decedent lived. A county newspaper is used only if there is no city newspaper or the decedent did not live in a city.Probate Hearing & AppointmentMonth 2-3Attend the probate hearingPresent will for admission to probateReceive court order appointing executor/administratorObtain Letters Testamentary or Letters of AdministrationOrder certified copies of Letters (the court charges $40 per certified copy plus $0.50 per page)Pro Tip: Letters Testamentary are essential - you'll need them to access bank accounts and manage assets.Asset Collection & NotificationMonths 3-4Open estate bank accountTransfer assets into estate nameNotify Social Security, pension providers, insurance companiesMail notice of administration to known creditors (within 4 months after Letters, or 30 days after you learn of a creditor, whichever is later)Within 90 days after Letters: notify the Franchise Tax Board, the Department of Health Care Services (if the decedent or the decedent's late spouse had Medi-Cal), the Victim Compensation Board (if an heir or beneficiary is or has been in prison or jail) and the Department of Child Support Services (if the decedent owed court-ordered child support)Begin collecting debts owed to the estateSecure and insure real propertyPro Tip: Keep detailed records of all transactions - you'll need them for the final accounting.Creditor Claim PeriodMonths 4-7Wait for creditor claims (4 months after Letters, or 60 days after a mailed notice if later)File the Inventory and Appraisal within 4 months after Letters, with the certification that the change in ownership statement (BOE-502-D) was filed with the county assessorReview and evaluate any claims receivedPay valid creditor claims from estate fundsReject invalid or excessive claimsContinue managing estate assetsFile federal estate tax return if required (due 9 months after death)Pro Tip: This waiting period cannot be shortened. It is set by California law.Real Property Sale (If Applicable)Months 5-8Obtain property appraisalList property for saleReview and accept offersWith full independent administration powers: give a Notice of Proposed Action at least 15 days before the sale (required for any sale of real estate)Without those powers: ask the court to confirm the sale (the court cannot confirm a private sale below 90% of the appraised value)Complete sale and deposit proceeds into estate accountPro Tip: Court confirmation is required unless the executor has full independent administration powers. With those powers, a Notice of Proposed Action is still required for any sale.Final Inventory & Tax ReturnsMonths 8-12File final income tax returns for decedentFile estate income tax returns if applicablePay any outstanding taxesObtain tax clearance from FTB and IRS if neededPro Tip: Hire a CPA experienced with estate taxation to ensure compliance and minimize taxes.Final Accounting & PetitionMonths 10-15Prepare the accounting of all receipts and disbursements (optional add-on with our service)Calculate statutory fees for executor and attorneyPrepare proposed distribution planFile Petition for Final DistributionMail notice to all interested partiesSchedule final hearingPro Tip: Accurate accounting is crucial - errors can delay distribution by months.Distribution & ClosingMonths 12-18 (petition or status report due within 1 year after Letters)Attend final hearing for court approvalReceive Order for Final DistributionDistribute assets to beneficiariesObtain receipts from all beneficiariesFile final receipts with the courtReceive Order Discharging ExecutorPro Tip: Keep copies of all signed receipts - they protect you from future claims.Common Causes of Probate DelaysWhile the timeline above represents a typical probate case, several factors can significantly extend the process. Being aware of these potential delays can help you plan and potentially avoid them.Will Contests+6-24+ monthsIf someone challenges the validity of the will, probate essentially pauses until the dispute is resolved through mediation, settlement, or trial.Missing Heirs+3-12 monthsIf beneficiaries cannot be located, the court may require extensive search efforts and publication before proceeding.Real Property Issues+3-6 monthsClouded titles, boundary disputes, or difficulties selling property can significantly extend the timeline.Tax Complications+3-12 monthsComplex tax situations, audits, or disputes with tax authorities can delay final distribution.Creditor Disputes+2-6 monthsIf creditors file claims that must be litigated, resolution can take several additional months.Court Backlogs+1-4 monthsSome California counties have significant court backlogs, especially in larger urban areas like Los Angeles.How to Speed Up the Probate ProcessWhile you cannot eliminate the mandatory waiting periods, there are several strategies to minimize delays and keep your probate case moving efficiently.1File PromptlyDon't delay starting the process. Deliver the original will to the court clerk within 30 days after learning of the death, and file the petition promptly to get your hearing date scheduled. Learn more in our step-by-step filing guide.2Hire an Experienced Probate AttorneyAn attorney who regularly practices in your specific court knows the local rules, judges' preferences, and how to avoid common mistakes that cause delays. Our flat-fee probate service prepares your court documents at each stage.3Organize Documents EarlyGather all necessary documents before filing: death certificate, original will, asset statements, beneficiary information, and creditor details. Missing documents cause delays.4Respond Quickly to Court RequestsWhen the court requests additional information or documents, respond immediately. Delays in responding can push your case to the back of the queue.5Communicate with BeneficiariesKeep all heirs and beneficiaries informed throughout the process. Clear communication can prevent disputes and objections that delay distribution.6Handle Real Property StrategicallyIf selling real estate, list it early in the process. With full independent administration powers, a sale needs a Notice of Proposed Action but no court confirmation, which saves time.Visual Probate Timeline Overview1FilingMonth 12HearingMonth 2-33Creditor Period4 Months (Required)4AccountingMonth 8-125DistributionMonth 12-18Typical estimate: 9 to 18 months | Complex estates: often longerFrequently Asked Questions About Probate TimelineHow long does probate take in California?Many California probate cases take about 9 to 18 months; complex estates can take longer. These are estimates. By law, creditors have at least 4 months after Letters to file claims, and the executor must ask the court to close the estate or file a status report within one year after Letters are issued.What is the creditor claim period in California probate?Creditors can file claims until 4 months after Letters Testamentary are issued, or 60 days after a mailed notice of administration if that is later. This period cannot be shortened.Can probate be expedited in California?While the creditor claim period cannot be shortened, you can speed up other phases by filing documents promptly, responding quickly to court requests, and working with experienced probate attorneys who know the local court procedures.What happens if probate takes longer than expected?If probate extends beyond initial expectations, beneficiaries must wait for their inheritances. The executor continues to manage the estate and may need to file status reports with the court. In some cases, the executor can request permission to make partial distributions to beneficiaries while the case is pending.How much does probate cost for an 18-month case?California statutory probate fees are based on estate value, not duration. However, longer cases may incur additional "extraordinary fees" for complex matters. Our flat-fee service ($3,995 full probate, $2,495 simplified) covers all standard probate work regardless of how long the case takes.Need Help Navigating the Probate Timeline?Our experienced team handles California probate cases every day. We know how to keep your case moving efficiently through each phase, minimizing delays and reducing stress.Start Your Case OnlineRelated ArticlesHow to File Probate in CaliforniaStep-by-step guide to starting the probate process.Small Estate Affidavit CaliforniaLearn when you can skip probate entirely.Letters Testamentary GuideEssential document for managing estate assets.Rozsa Gyene, Esq.California State Bar #208356 • 26+ Years ExperienceRozsa Gyene focuses on California probate administration, with extensive experience at the Stanley Mosk Courthouse in Los Angeles.Verify License Need Help With Your Probate Case?Get attorney-prepared court papers for a flat fee: $3,995 for full probate or $2,495 for the simplified home petition.Explore Our Probate Services→ How Our Process Works→ Probate FAQ (50+ Questions)→ 35 California Locations→ Los Angeles Probate→ San Francisco Probate→ San Diego ProbateBack to Learning Center

articles.title: What Happens If You Die Without a Will in California? Intestate Succession Explained
articles.text: When someone dies without a valid will in California, their estate doesn't simply go to whoever wants it. Instead, California's intestate succession laws dictate exactly who inherits, and the results often surprise families.Common MisconceptionMany people believe that dying without a will means "the state takes everything." This is almost never true. California has a detailed system for distributing assets to relatives: the state only inherits when absolutely no family can be found.What is Intestate Succession?"Intestate" means dying without a valid will. When this happens, California Probate Code Section 6400 and subsequent sections determine who inherits. This body of law is called intestate succession.The rules create a strict hierarchy of inheritance based on family relationships. Your closest relatives inherit first, and more distant relatives only inherit if closer relatives don't exist.Who Inherits Under California Intestate Succession?The distribution depends on your family situation. Here's how California law prioritizes heirs:If You're Married (With or Without Children)California distinguishes between community property and separate property:Community PropertyProperty acquired during marriage100% goes to surviving spouseSeparate PropertyProperty owned before marriage or received as gift/inheritanceSplit depends on children/relatives (see table below)Separate Property DistributionFamily SituationSpouse ReceivesOthers ReceiveSpouse + 1 child1/2Child gets 1/2Spouse + 2+ children1/3Children share 2/3 equallySpouse + no children, but parents1/2Parents get 1/2Spouse + no children, but siblings1/2Siblings share 1/2Spouse only (no children, parents, or siblings)100%-If You're NOT MarriedWithout a spouse, inheritance follows this order:1Children (and descendants of deceased children)Divided equally among children. If a child died, their children inherit their share.2ParentsIf no children, parents inherit equally (or surviving parent gets all).3Siblings (and descendants of deceased siblings)If no children or parents, siblings share equally.4Grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousinsThe law continues through increasingly distant relatives.∞State of California (Escheat)Only if absolutely no relatives can be found after diligent search.Important Rules to KnowHalf-Relatives Inherit EquallyHalf-siblings are treated the same as full siblings under California law.Adopted Children Have Full RightsLegally adopted children inherit exactly like biological children.Stepchildren Do NOT InheritUnless legally adopted, stepchildren have no inheritance rights under intestate succession.Unmarried Partners Inherit NOTHINGDomestic partners registered with the state are treated like spouses, but unmarried couples have zero inheritance rights.Do You Still Need Probate Without a Will?Yes: Probate is Still RequiredA common myth is that having no will means no probate. In reality, intestate estates almost always require probate, and the process is often more complicated because:The court must determine who the rightful heirs areAn administrator must be appointed (instead of an executor named in a will)A probate bond is required unless all heirs waive it in writing (a will can also waive it)Finding and notifying all potential heirs takes more timeWhat Assets Pass Outside of Intestate Succession?Not all assets are distributed through intestate succession. These assets pass directly to named beneficiaries:Pass to Named Beneficiaries• Life insurance policies• Retirement accounts (401k, IRA)• Payable-on-death bank accounts• Transfer-on-death securities• Property in a living trust• Joint tenancy propertySubject to Intestate Succession• Bank accounts in decedent's name only• Real estate in decedent's name only• Vehicles titled solely to decedent• Personal property (furniture, jewelry)• Business interests• Investment accounts without TODReal-World ExampleScenario: John dies without a willJohn was married to Maria and had two adult children from a previous marriage. His estate includes:• Family home (community property with Maria): $800,000• Inheritance from his mother (separate property): $300,000• 401(k) with Maria as beneficiary: $200,000How it's distributed:• Family home: 100% to Maria (community property)• 401(k): 100% to Maria (named beneficiary)• $300,000 inheritance: Maria gets 1/3 ($100,000), children split 2/3 ($100,000 each)Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat if the deceased was separated but not divorced?Legally, they're still married. The separated spouse has full inheritance rights under intestate succession until the divorce is finalized.Can I inherit if I killed the deceased?No. California's "slayer statute" (Probate Code § 250) prevents anyone who feloniously kills the decedent from inheriting from them.What about children born outside of marriage?They have full inheritance rights as long as paternity was legally established (through acknowledgment, court order, or genetic testing).How long does intestate probate take?Often about 9 to 18 months (an estimate), sometimes longer if heir identification is complicated. See our probate timeline guide for details.Need Help With an Intestate Estate?Administering an estate without a will can be complicated. articles.title: Executor Duties in California Probate: Complete Responsibilities Guide
articles.text: Being named executor of a California estate is both an honor and a significant responsibility. As executor (also called "personal representative"), you're legally obligated to manage the estate, protect its assets, pay debts, and distribute property to beneficiaries, all while navigating California's probate court system.Executor vs. AdministratorAn executor is named in a will. An administrator is appointed by the court when there's no will or the named executor can't serve. The duties are essentially identical: only the appointment process differs.Your Core Fiduciary DutiesAs executor, you have a fiduciary duty to the estate and its beneficiaries. This is the highest legal duty of care and means you must:Duty of LoyaltyAct solely in the interest of the beneficiaries, never for personal gain. Avoid conflicts of interest.Duty of CareManage estate assets prudently. Make informed decisions. Seek professional help when needed.Duty to AccountKeep detailed records of all transactions. Provide accountings to the court and beneficiaries.Duty of ImpartialityTreat all beneficiaries fairly. Don't favor one heir over another unless the will specifies.Complete Executor Responsibilities Checklist1Immediate Actions (First 30 Days)Locate the original willCheck safe deposit boxes, home safes, the decedent's attorney, or the county clerk.Obtain several certified death certificatesYou'll need these for banks, title companies, insurance, and government agencies.Secure all estate propertyChange locks if needed, collect valuables, redirect mail, secure vehicles.Notify Social Security, pension providers, employersStop benefits to avoid overpayments that must be repaid.Contact a probate attorneyGet guidance on whether probate is needed and understand the process.2Opening Probate (Months 1-2)File Petition for Probate (Form DE-111)Submit to the Superior Court in the county where the decedent lived.Post probate bond (if required)Not required if the will waives it or all beneficiaries waive it in writing, though the court can still require one. Full independent administration powers over real estate can raise the bond amount.Notify heirs and beneficiariesMail Notice of Petition (Form DE-121) at least 15 days before hearing.Publish notice in local newspaperThe notice of petition is published three times before the hearing, the first at least 15 days before it.Attend probate hearingThe court will formally appoint you and issue Letters Testamentary.3Estate Administration (Months 2-12)Open estate bank accountDeposit estate funds here. Never commingle with personal funds.Inventory all assetsCreate a complete list of real property, bank accounts, investments, personal property.Work with probate referee for appraisalsThe court-appointed referee values most non-cash assets.File Inventory and Appraisal (Form DE-160)Due within 4 months after Letters are issued. File it with the certification that the change in ownership statement (BOE-502-D) was filed for any California real estate.Notify known creditorsMail the Notice of Administration to Creditors (Form DE-157) within 4 months after Letters are issued, or within 30 days after you learn of a creditor, whichever is later.Review and pay valid creditor claimsCreditors have 4 months to file claims. Evaluate each claim carefully.Manage ongoing expensesPay mortgage, utilities, insurance, property taxes from estate funds.File tax returnsFinal personal return (Form 1040), estate income tax (Form 1041), and estate tax (Form 706) if applicable.4Closing the Estate (Final Months)Prepare final accountingDocument all receipts, disbursements, and distributions.File Petition for Final DistributionRequest court approval to distribute remaining assets to beneficiaries.Distribute assets to beneficiariesTransfer property, write checks, and obtain receipts from each beneficiary.File receipts with courtProve that beneficiaries received their distributions.Request discharge from dutiesThe court officially releases you from your executor role.Executor Compensation in CaliforniaUnder California Probate Code Section 10800, executors are entitled to statutory compensation:Statutory Executor FeesFirst $100,000 of estate value4%Next $100,0003%Next $800,0002%Next $9,000,0001%Next $15,000,0000.5%Above $25,000,000Set by the courtExample: For a $500,000 estate: $4,000 + $3,000 + $6,000 = $13,000 executor feeExecutor Fees Are Taxable IncomeUnlike inheritances (which are tax-free), executor compensation is taxable as ordinary income. Many family member executors choose to waive fees, especially if they're also beneficiaries.Personal Liability RisksExecutors can be held personally liable for:Mismanaging assets: Letting property deteriorate, making bad investments, or losing estate fundsPremature distributions: Distributing assets before paying all debts and taxesMissing tax deadlines: Failing to file returns or pay taxes on timeSelf-dealing: Using estate assets for personal benefitIgnoring creditors: Distributing assets without properly addressing valid claimsProtect YourselfThe best way to avoid liability is to: (1) keep meticulous records, (2) get court approval before major decisions, (3) work with a probate attorney, and (4) never commingle estate funds with personal funds.Frequently Asked QuestionsCan I decline to be an executor?Yes. Being named in a will doesn't obligate you to serve. You can renounce (decline) before the court appoints you. Once appointed, you can petition to resign, but the court must approve.Can there be multiple executors?Yes. Co-executors must generally act together and agree on decisions. This can provide checks and balances but may also create conflict. The statutory fee is not paid in full to each co-executor. One fee is shared among them, as the court decides based on the work each did, or as they agree.Can an executor also be a beneficiary?Absolutely. It's very common for a spouse or child to serve as both executor and primary beneficiary. However, you must still fulfill all duties impartially and document everything carefully.What if beneficiaries disagree with my decisions?Beneficiaries can file objections with the probate court. The court will review your actions and determine if they were appropriate. Always document your reasoning for major decisions.How long does probate take?Many California probate cases take about 9 to 18 months (an estimate, not a legal deadline). See our complete probate timeline guide for month-by-month details.Overwhelmed by Executor Duties?You don't have to do this alone. Our experienced probate attorneys guide executors through every step of the process for a flat fee of $3,995 ($2,495 for the simplified home petition). We prepare the court papers and track the deadlines, so you can focus on your family.Get Executor Support TodayRozsa Gyene, Esq.California State Bar #208356 • 26+ Years ExperienceRozsa Gyene focuses on California probate administration, with extensive experience at the Stanley Mosk Courthouse in Los Angeles.Verify License Need Help With Your Probate Case?Get attorney-prepared court papers for a flat fee: $3,995 for full probate or $2,495 for the simplified home petition.Explore Our Probate Services→ How Our Process Works→ Probate FAQ (50+ Questions)→ 35 California Locations→ Los Angeles Probate→ San Francisco Probate→ San Diego ProbateRelated ArticlesStep-by-Step GuideHow to File Probate in CaliforniaExecutor GuideProbate Bond Requirements CaliforniaForms & DocumentsLetters Testamentary California GuideBack to Learning Center
